title: M/S DHANLAXMI MERCHANDISE PVT. LTD. VS. STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1125
SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 1 of 56
NON-REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).13749 OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No. 11388 of 2026)
M/S DHANLAXMI MERCHANDISE
PVT. LTD. ... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
& ORS. ...RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).13750 OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No. 11160 of 2026)
SAHAKAR GLOBAL LTD. ... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
& ORS. ...RESPONDENT(S)
J U D G M E N T
ARAVIND KUMAR, J.
1. Leave granted.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 2 of 56
2. These appeals arise from a common judgment dated
18.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Jabalpur in Writ Petition No.48901 of 2025 and Writ Petition
No.1880 of 2026. The former writ petition was instituted by
Sahakar Global Limited (hereinafter referred to as "Sahakar"
for brevity) and concerns the sand mining group of District
Shahdol, while the latter was instituted by M/s Dhanlaxmi
Merchandise Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as
"Dhanlaxmi" for brevity) and concerns the sand mining group
of District Katni. In both proceedings, challenge was laid to the
cancellation of an e-tender-cum-auction conducted by the
Madhya Pradesh State Mining Corporation Limited pursuant
to Notice No. Sand/Tender/2025-26/406 dated 18.09.2025.
The cancellation in respect of the two groups flowed from a
common decision taken by the Board of Directors of the
Corporation on 19.11.2025 and was communicated to the
concerned bidders on 05.12.2025. Since the two writ petitions
arose out of the same decision and raised substantially common
questions, they were heard and disposed of together by the
High Court. These appeals have accordingly been heard
together, though certain facts peculiar to the two appellants
require separate consideration.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 3 of 56
3. The circumstances in which the controversy arose may be
stated at the outset. Both appellants had, under an earlier round
of tendering, operated the very sand groups for which they
subsequently bid. Both surrendered those contracts under the
surrender provision then in force. The Corporation thereafter
brought Shahdol and Katni again to auction, accepted the
appellants as technically qualified participants and conducted
the competitive bidding to its conclusion. Sahakar emerged as
the highest bidder for Shahdol and Dhanlaxmi for Katni. The
amounts quoted by them in the fresh auction were, however,
substantially lower than the amounts which they had
themselves quoted in the earlier round. It was this
circumstance, read with the fact of surrender, which led the
Board to reconsider whether the tender process ought to be
carried further.
4. The factual position of the two appellants is not altogether
identical. Sahakar's earlier Shahdol contract had already
become the subject matter of proceedings concerning
availability of mines with the requisite statutory permissions
before the surrender was tendered. The Katni contract of
Dhanlaxmi does not carry the same history. It would, therefore,
be appropriate first to notice the statutory arrangement and

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 4 of 56
thereafter the factual course of the two contracts separately
before they converge in the common tender of September
2025.
STATUTORY AND CONTRACTUAL SETTING
5. The Madhya Pradesh Sand (Mining, Transportation, Storage
and Trading) Rules, 2019 govern the extraction, transportation,
storage and trading of sand in the State. The Rules were
materially amended on 26.05.2023. Under the arrangement
introduced by that amendment, the quarry leases came to be
allotted to the Madhya Pradesh State Mining Corporation
Limited, which was to carry out mining operations through
Mine Developer-cum-Operators (hereinafter referred to as
"MDO" for brevity) selected in accordance with the prescribed
procedure. The Corporation thus remained the holder of the
quarry leases, while the MDO selected for a particular group
undertook the mining and sale operations subject to the
statutory permissions governing the individual mines.
6. The regulatory arrangement contemplated that the mining plan,
environmental clearance and the requisite water and air
consents would govern actual extraction. A mine could form
part of a notified group although all permissions might not have

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 5 of 56
become operative at the same point of time. Inclusion of a mine
in the tendered group and the entitlement actually to extract
mineral therefrom were, therefore, matters which had to be
understood with reference to the permissions then in force.
7. Rule 7 prescribed the manner in which the initial base or upset
price was to be worked out, while Rule 8 provided for selection
through e-tender-cum-e-auction. Rule 9 contemplated a
contract for three years. The bid amounts which figure
prominently in these proceedings were annual bid amounts and
not the aggregate consideration for the full three-year tenure.
The fresh tender which later came to be issued was not merely
for the unexpired residue of the earlier surrendered agreements;
it contemplated a fresh contractual tenure under the Rules.
8. Rule 16, in the form in which it stood during 2025, permitted
an MDO to surrender a sand group by giving three months'
advance notice to the Corporation, subject to payment of the
dues payable to the Corporation and the State Government and
approval of the State Government. The application, once
submitted, was irrevocable and possession was thereafter to be
handed over in accordance with the agreement. Upon receipt
of the surrender application, the Corporation was required to
initiate proceedings for re-tendering the group. An application

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 6 of 56
within the last six months of the contractual period was not to
be considered.
9. The Rule as it then stood did not prescribe a general
disqualification preventing the surrendering MDO from
participating when the same group was re-tendered. Nor did it
stipulate that such an MDO, if otherwise eligible, could
participate only upon offering an amount equal to or greater
than its earlier bid. This position was subsequently altered by
amendment dated 30.01.2026, to which we shall advert at the
appropriate stage.
10. The tender conditions themselves also reserved substantial
powers in favour of the Corporation. Clause 6.5.5 dealt with
determination of the H1 participant, while Clauses 6.6.3 and 26
reserved to the competent authority the power to reject the
highest bid and to cancel the tender process. Emergence as H1
did not, therefore, amount to an unconditional acceptance or a
concluded contract. At the same time, those clauses formed
part of a tender issued by a State instrumentality and their
operation remained subject to the law governing exercise of
public power.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 7 of 56
SHAHDOL AND SAHAKAR GLOBAL LIMITED
11. The Shahdol group comprised 34 mines with an annual
tendered quantity of 17,60,000 cubic metres. The reserve price
under the earlier tender was ₹44 crore. Sahakar Global Limited
emerged successful in that process with an annual bid of
₹68,84,25,999, corresponding to approximately ₹391.151 per
cubic metre. An agreement was executed between Sahakar and
the Corporation on 12.01.2024 for a three-year period ending
on 11.01.2027.
12. Difficulties thereafter arose in the operation of that agreement.
The Corporation's own pleadings disclose that environmental
clearances had been obtained for 23 mines corresponding to
approximately 14,86,630 cubic metres, as against the 34 mines
and annual tendered quantity of 17,60,000 cubic metres
forming part of the notified group. Sahakar's stand was that it
had bid for the whole notified group upon the expectation that
the mines comprising it would be made available with the
requisite statutory permissions. The Corporation maintained,
on the other hand, that the tender conditions sufficiently
disclosed the permission position and that Sahakar had

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 8 of 56
undertaken the commercial venture after acquainting itself
with the mines and the applicable conditions.
13. This disagreement was not raised for the first time after the
later tender came to be cancelled. Sahakar had already
approached the High Court by instituting Writ Petition
No.15714 of 2025. By an interim order dated 09.05.2025, the
High Court directed, pending further consideration, that
Sahakar should continue to make payment having regard to the
quantity actually extracted from the available quantity for
which environmental clearance had been received. The interim
arrangement did not finally determine that the Corporation was
in breach, nor did it adjudicate Sahakar's ultimate financial
liability under the agreement. It nevertheless forms an
important part of the chronology because the controversy
concerning permissions was already alive before the surrender
which followed.
14. On 11.07.2025, Sahakar submitted a notice of surrender. The
communication referred to the difficulty arising from non-availability of statutory permissions for the entire tendered
quantity and to the financial consequences which, according to
the appellant, had resulted therefrom. The surrender was
sought under the provision then governing the relationship.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 9 of 56
The Corporation's own surrender chart records 10.10.2025 as
the effective date of surrender. We are not concerned in these
proceedings with the final settlement of accounts under that
earlier agreement.
KATNI AND DHANLAXMI MERCHANDISE PRIVATE
LIMITED
15. The Katni group comprised 49 mines with an annual tendered
quantity of 20,00,000 cubic metres. The reserve price under the
earlier process was ₹50 crore. Dhanlaxmi Merchandise Private
Limited emerged successful at an annual bid of ₹64,77,66,000,
corresponding to approximately ₹323.883 per cubic metre. The
agreement between Dhanlaxmi and the Corporation was
executed on 01.11.2023 for a period of three years.
16. Dhanlaxmi submitted its notice of surrender on 01.08.2025.
The communication invoked the provision permitting
surrender on three months' notice and stated that there were no
outstanding dues. The Corporation's chart records 31.10.2025
as the effective date of surrender. Unlike Shahdol, no
corresponding dispute concerning absence of environmental
clearance for the Katni mines had arisen. The Corporation has

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 10 of 56
specifically maintained that the requisite permissions for Katni
were available.
17. In its later pleadings, Dhanlaxmi attributed the surrender to the
commercial working of the contract, including demand,
transportation and operational costs and the actual quantities
which could be sold. Its rejoinder referred to sales of 8,60,970
cubic metres during the first contractual year and 16,81,512
cubic metres during the second, against the annual tendered
quantity of 20,00,000 cubic metres. Those figures form part of
the appellant's pleaded explanation and are not findings
resulting from an audit of the earlier contract. It is also
significant that the surrender notice itself did not set out that
commercial explanation in the detail subsequently found in the
rejoinder.
18. At this stage, therefore, the factual courses of Shahdol and
Katni remained distinct. What brought them together was the
decision of the Corporation to place both groups again in the
market.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 11 of 56
DECISION TO RE-TENDER
19. Before the fresh NIT was issued, the question of strengthening
the surrender provisions had already engaged the attention of
the authorities. Proposals were under consideration for
restricting participation by surrendering MDOs, recovering
loss arising upon re-tendering and introducing stricter
consequences in cases of surrender.
20. The matter was considered at the 281st meeting of the Board
held on 18.09.2025. The Board was conscious of the proposed
changes and of the fact that certain groups, including Shahdol
and Katni, had been surrendered. It nevertheless resolved that,
in order to ensure continuity in the supply of sand, selection of
MDOs for Katni, Shahdol, Jabalpur, Guna, Barwani, Rajgarh
and Mandsaur could be undertaken under the Rules then
prevailing. This contemporaneous decision is reflected in the
Board material forming part of the record.
21. On the same date, the Corporation issued Notice No.
Sand/Tender/2025-26/406. The detailed tender material
followed on 19.09.2025 and the schedule was thereafter
modified by a corrigendum dated 24.09.2025. Shahdol
continued to be notified with 34 mines, an annual quantity of

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 12 of 56
17,60,000 cubic metres and a reserve price of ₹44 crore. Katni
was notified with 49 mines, an annual quantity of 20,00,000
cubic metres and a reserve price of ₹50 crore.
22. Both appellants participated in the process. Their technical bids
were scrutinised and accepted. The material later placed before
the Board records seven technically qualified participants for
Shahdol and five for Katni. The tender was therefore not
proceeding with a solitary eligible bidder in either district.
AUCTION DATED 10.10.2025
23. The financial auctions were held on 10.10.2025. For Shahdol,
Sahakar submitted the highest initial price offer of
₹46,80,00,000. The electronic auction commenced at 11.00
a.m. Other participants thereafter entered higher bids and the
bidding continued until Sahakar submitted its final offer of
₹48,20,40,000 at 12.34 p.m. The amount remained the highest
offer at closure. On the annual quantity of 17,60,000 cubic
metres, the resulting rate was approximately ₹273.886 per
cubic metre. The annual offer exceeded the reserve price of ₹44
crore by ₹4,20,40,000.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 13 of 56
24. In Katni, the highest initial offer was ₹52,37,11,111. The
auction commenced at 10.00 a.m. Sahakar, which was itself a
participant in the Katni process, submitted a higher bid at 10.48
a.m. Successive bids followed and the process culminated in
Dhanlaxmi's offer of ₹54,07,41,111 at 11.36 a.m. This
remained H1 at closure. The amount corresponded to
approximately ₹270.371 per cubic metre and exceeded the
reserve price of ₹50 crore by ₹4,07,41,111.
25. Sahakar thus emerged H1 for Shahdol and Dhanlaxmi H1 for
Katni. No Letter of Intent or final allotment was issued
immediately thereafter.
LEGAL OPINION AND BOARD CONSIDERATION
26. The Corporation thereafter sought legal advice by a
communication dated 31.10.2025. The opinion dated
11.11.2025, as reproduced in the Board agenda, records that
the successful bidders had neither been debarred nor
blacklisted; that the Corporation had stated that they complied
with the requirements of the current tender; and that no
document warranting an adverse inference against them had
accompanied the reference. The advice was that the
Corporation could proceed, subject to satisfaction of the

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 14 of 56
remaining tender and statutory requirements. The opinion did
not bind the Board and did not amount to acceptance of either
bid. Its relevance lies in the factual position obtaining when the
matter thereafter came up for decision.
27. At its meeting held on 19.11.2025, the Board considered the
results of the fresh auction together with the corresponding
figures under the earlier contracts. In Shahdol, the earlier
annual bid of ₹68,84,25,999 was compared with the fresh H1
bid of ₹48,20,40,000. The difference was ₹20,63,85,999, or
approximately 29.98 per cent. In Katni, the earlier annual bid
of ₹64,77,66,000 was compared with ₹54,07,41,111, yielding
a difference of ₹10,70,24,889, or approximately 16.52 per cent.
These were substantial differences.
28. In relation to Shahdol, the Board material also adverted to the
earlier dispute concerning statutory permissions and to the
Corporation's stand that the operative permission position had
not changed in the manner suggested by Sahakar. The tender
obligations concerning inspection of the mines and the bidder's
knowledge of the relevant circumstances were also referred to.
It would, therefore, not be correct to say that the permission
controversy was wholly absent from the material placed before
the Board.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 15 of 56
29. Upon consideration of the material, the Board formed the view
that the highest rates obtained in the fresh auction for Shahdol
and Katni were not competitive and resolved to reject the offers
and cancel the e-tender-cum-auction process for those two
groups. It did not declare either appellant ineligible or blacklist
them. Nor did it determine the liabilities, if any, under their
earlier surrendered agreements. The operative decision was
confined to rejection of the present bids and cancellation of the
fresh process.
30. The decision was communicated on 05.12.2025. The
cancellation communications themselves were brief and
referred to the power contained in the tender conditions. The
detailed basis upon which the Board had acted emerged from
the contemporaneous agenda and minutes subsequently placed
before the High Court.
PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT AND
AMENDMENT OF THE RULES
31. Sahakar questioned the cancellation by filing Writ Petition
No.48901 of 2025 in relation to Shahdol. Dhanlaxmi instituted
Writ Petition No.1880 of 2026 concerning Katni. Since both
challenges arose from the same Board decision, the

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 16 of 56
Corporation placed substantially common material before the
High Court, while also dealing with the factual features
particular to each district.
32. During pendency of those proceedings, the Sand Rules were
amended on 30.01.2026. The substituted Rule 16 introduced a
materially different surrender regime. Amongst other things, it
provided that the MDO, and its proprietor, director or partner,
which had surrendered a group would not be eligible to
participate in the e-tender-cum-auction of the same group for
the prescribed three-year period. Provision was also made for
adjustment of loss arising upon re-tendering against the
security of the former MDO and for recovery of any balance.
The upset-price methodology applicable to surrendered groups
was also altered.
33. Following the amendment, the Corporation issued another NIT
on 10.02.2026. The reserve price was fixed at ₹52.80 crore for
Shahdol and ₹60 crore for Katni. That subsequent process
assumed relevance later when the question of interim
protection and eventual relief came before this Court.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 17 of 56
JUDGMENT OF THE HIGH COURT
34. The two writ petitions were heard together and disposed of by
the common judgment dated 18.03.2026. The High Court
noticed that both Appellants had themselves obtained the
respective district groups at higher rates in the earlier round,
had thereafter surrendered those groups and had once again
emerged H1 in the fresh process at lower rates. It accepted the
Corporation's position that the difference was substantial and
that the decision to cancel the process was one taken in
protection of public revenue.
35. The High Court also relied upon Clauses 6.6.3 and 26 and upon
the settled principle that the highest bidder does not acquire an
indefeasible right to have the contract concluded in its favour.
It noticed the earlier litigation concerning Sahakar and the
environmental-clearance position, but did not regard the same
as sufficient to displace the commercial decision of the Board.
36. Reliance placed by the Appellant's upon Golden Food
Products India v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Others1 was
distinguished. The High Court understood the decision as
1
2026 SCC OnLine SC 24

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 18 of 56
recognising that the highest bid may be rejected for a valid
reason and held that the substantial difference between the
amounts quoted by the same MDOs in the two rounds, with the
attendant implications for public revenue, furnished such a
reason. Both writ petitions were accordingly dismissed.
PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THIS COURT
37. Sahakar thereafter preferred SLP(C) No.11160 of 2026, while
Dhanlaxmi preferred SLP(C) No.11388 of 2026. On
25.03.2026, this Court issued notice and directed that the fresh
auction process, insofar as Shahdol and Katni were concerned,
should not be finalised without leave of the Court. The matters
came to be heard on several dates thereafter. Since the two
petitions arose out of the common judgment and the same
Board decision, SLP(C) No.11388 of 2026 was directed to be
listed along with SLP(C) No.11160 of 2026.
38. During pendency of the proceedings, applications for
intervention and impleadment were filed by participants in the
subsequent Shahdol process. Material was placed on record
showing higher initial price offers in that later round. The
subsequent e-auction had, however, not culminated in a final
allotment on account of the interim order of this Court. Those

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 19 of 56
developments bear primarily upon the relief to be granted and
will be considered at the appropriate stage.
39. With this factual background, we may notice the submissions
advanced on behalf of the parties.
SUBMISSIONS AND CONTENTIONS OF PARTIES
ON BEHALF OF SAHAKAR GLOBAL LIMITED
40. Mr. K. Parameshwar, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
Sahakar Global Limited, submitted that the cancellation
proceeded upon an erroneous assumption that the earlier
annual bid of ₹68,84,25,999 represented the continuing value
of the Shahdol mining opportunity and could, without anything
further, be used as the benchmark for judging the
competitiveness of the September 2025 auction. Learned
Senior Counsel submitted that the two contractual situations
could not be treated as economically identical merely because
both concerned the Shahdol group.
41. He drew our attention to the position relating to statutory
permissions under the earlier agreement. The tendered group
comprised 34 mines and 17,60,000 cubic metres, whereas the
Corporation's own pleadings recorded environmental

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 20 of 56
clearances for 23 mines corresponding to approximately
14,86,630 cubic metres. It was submitted that Sahakar had bid
for the notified opportunity, whereas in practice the entire
tendered group had not become available for lawful mining.
42. Learned Senior Counsel further submitted that this was not a
grievance raised after the surrender. Sahakar had approached
the High Court in Writ Petition No.15714 of 2025 and had
obtained the interim order dated 09.05.2025 relating payment
to actual extraction from the available quantity for which
environmental clearance had been received. The surrender
dated 11.07.2025 followed thereafter. According to him, the
earlier bid could not therefore be treated as an unquestioned
indication of the commercial value subsequently available
under the fresh tender.
43. It was next submitted that Sahakar had exercised a right which
the law then expressly recognised. Rule 16 permitted surrender
and required re-tendering. There was no provision at the
relevant time disqualifying the surrendering MDO from
participating again. Sahakar had not been blacklisted or
debarred, and the Corporation itself found it technically
eligible under the fresh NIT.

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 21 of 56
44. Learned Senior Counsel laid particular emphasis on the Board
decision dated 18.09.2025. He submitted that the Board was
already conscious that amendments to the surrender regime
were under consideration, yet consciously decided to proceed
with selection under the Rules then prevailing. Having done so,
the Corporation could not, after completion of the auction, treat
the appellant as though a restriction subsequently introduced in
January 2026 were already part of the September 2025 regime.
45. He thereafter took us through the actual bidding record. Seven
bidders had qualified for Shahdol. Sahakar's initial offer was
₹46.80 crore and the electronic auction thereafter witnessed
successive bids before Sahakar emerged H1 at ₹48,20,40,000.
The final figure exceeded the reserve price by ₹4,20,40,000.
There was no allegation of collusion, cartelisation or
manipulation of the auction. In such circumstances, it was
submitted, the conclusion that the result was "non-competitive" merely because Sahakar had earlier quoted more
could not be sustained.
46. Learned Senior Counsel also referred to the legal opinion dated
11.11.2025, which recorded that the successful bidders were
neither debarred nor blacklisted and that no adverse material

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 22 of 56
had been furnished to the law officer. He fairly accepted that
the opinion did not bind the Board, but submitted that it
demonstrated the factual position immediately preceding the
impugned decision.
47. The subsequent amendment dated 30.01.2026 was also relied
upon. Learned Senior Counsel submitted that the rule-making
authority then expressly introduced the very restriction which
had not existed earlier, namely ineligibility of the surrendering
MDO and its connected persons for the same group for the
prescribed period, coupled with a mechanism for recovery of
loss. The amendment being prospective, it could not furnish a
disqualification for an auction already conducted under the
earlier regime.
48. Reliance was placed upon Food Corporation of India v. M/s.
Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries2
, Tata Cellular v. Union of
India 3
, M.P. Power Management Company Limited,
Jabalpur v. Sky Power Southeast Solar India Private Limited
and Others 4
, Subodh Kumar Singh Rathour v. Chief
2
(1993) 1 SCC 71
3
(1994) 6 SCC 651
4
(2023) 2 SCC 703

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 23 of 56
Executive Officer and Others 5 and Golden Food Products
India v. State of Uttar Pradesh (supra). Learned Senior
Counsel clarified that the appellant was not asserting an
absolute right merely because it was H1. The submission was
that, once a public authority conducted a valid competitive
process and received an above-reserve H1 offer, rejection of
that result had to rest upon material rationally demonstrating
why the offer was unacceptable. A bidder's own historical
offer, without an assessment of comparability and current
value, could not by itself supply that basis.
49. Lastly, learned Senior Counsel submitted that the subsequent
Shahdol process could not retrospectively validate the earlier
cancellation. The later process arose under an amended regime,
at an enhanced reserve price and at a later point of time. In any
event, no final competitive allotment had arisen from that
process owing to the interim order of this court.
ON BEHALF OF DHANLAXMI MERCHANDISE PRIVATE
LIMITED
50. Mr. Balbir Singh, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
Dhanlaxmi Merchandise Private Limited, adopted the
5
(2024) 15 SCC 461

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 24 of 56
submissions concerning the scope of judicial review, the old
Rule 16 and the prospective amendment, but submitted that
Katni stood on its own factual footing. He did not seek to place
Dhanlaxmi upon the particular environmental-clearance
dispute which existed in Shahdol.
51. Learned Senior Counsel submitted that Dhanlaxmi had
obtained Katni at the earlier annual bid of ₹64,77,66,000 and
thereafter surrendered the group on 01.08.2025 under the
provision then in force. No breach of eligibility attached to the
surrender. The Corporation itself thereafter placed Katni for
fresh auction and accepted Dhanlaxmi as technically qualified.
52. Five bidders were qualified in Katni and the e-auction
generated successive bids. Sahakar itself participated in the
auction and entered a higher bid during the process. Dhanlaxmi
ultimately emerged H1 at ₹54,07,41,111, exceeding the reserve
price of ₹50 crore by ₹4,07,41,111. Learned Senior Counsel
submitted that there was no factual basis upon which such a
process could be described as devoid of competition.
53. It was urged that the mere fact that Dhanlaxmi had previously
offered ₹64.77 crore could not turn that amount into a
permanent minimum price for Katni. An earlier bidder which

SLP (C) No.11388 of 2026 with
SLP (C) No.11160 of 2026 Page 25 of 56
had misjudged the commercial potential of a contract remained
liable for its earlier obligations until surrender took effect in
accordance with law, but its earlier commercial judgment could
not bind every future auction.
54. Learned Senior Counsel referred to the appellant's pleaded
experience relating to demand, transportation costs,
operational expenses and actual quantities sold under the
earlier contract. He clarified, however, that the appellant's case
did not depend upon establishing fault on the part of the
Corporation. Rule 16 did not require an MDO to prove breach
by the Corporation before exercising the surrender facility.
55. Attention was also drawn to the material concerning Mandla,
Anuppur and Balaghat, where subsequent tender values were
said to have been materially lower than the corresponding
earlier amounts. It was not submitted that the economics of
every district were identical. The material was relied upon to
demonstrate that a lower price following surrender had not,
under the earlier regime, invariably been treated as proof that
the later auction was unacceptable.

106. The higher initial figures said to have been received in the
later Shahdol process do not persuade us to preserve that

those figures arose in a different regulatory setting and after
